## Note S1. Drivers of technical inefficiency

Table S7 reports the covariates entering the inefficiency term, estimated on the naive national
frontier, on each group-specific frontier, and on the matched and unmatched meta-frontiers. A
positive coefficient moves the farm away from its efficient frontier; age and education enter in
logs and are therefore elasticities. Three features of that table bear on how the ownership results
in Section 5 should be read.

The first concerns gender. On all three single-technology frontiers (the naive national frontier
and both group-specific frontiers), being a female farmer is associated with significantly greater
inefficiency, and the coefficient is larger among non-owners than among owners. This is the most
consistent farmer-level result in the table, and it is worth stating plainly that it does not
disappear once ownership is held constant: whatever it reflects, it is not a by-product of women
being less likely to own the land they farm.

The second concerns what is absent. Extension contact and mechanization carry no significant
coefficient on any frontier, in either direction, and neither does age or crop diversification.
Credit access is significant on the naive frontier and among owners, but with a positive sign: farmers with credit sit further from the frontier, not closer. We do not read this causally. Credit
in these rounds reaches a small minority of farmers (Table 1), is not randomly assigned, and is
plausibly sought by farms already under production stress; the sign is as consistent with selection
into borrowing as with any effect of borrowing on performance.

The third concerns the meta-frontier columns, where no covariate reaches conventional significance
and the jackknife standard errors are substantially larger than on the single-technology frontiers.
The natural reading is that once technology heterogeneity between ownership groups is modelled
separately, rather than absorbed into a single national frontier, farmer attributes explain little
of the residual inefficiency, the same conflation the meta-frontier framework exists to resolve,
and part of why this paper reports technology gap ratios and technical efficiency separately rather
than as a single productivity index. That reading should be held loosely. The meta-frontier
estimates are imprecise enough that the table cannot distinguish small effects from none, and the
nulls there are better described as uninformative than as evidence of no relationship.

One caution applies throughout. The inefficiency model is estimated jointly with the frontier, so
its coefficients are conditional on the frontier specification. Figure S2 shows that the assumed
distribution of the inefficiency term is the dimension to which the aggregate ownership results are
most sensitive; the signs reported here are stable across the matching and functional-form
dimensions and should not be assumed robust to distributional choice.

```{r, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
sec_landscape()
```
